# LuthorSQL: A One-Pass Text-to-SQL Model as System 1 for a Slower LLM Agent

## Research question

Routing easier database questions to a local generator may reduce agent cost, but a confidence gate must account for wrong high-confidence queries and stronger-agent gains.

## Method

One generator pass fills bounded plan slots; a deterministic compiler constructs SQL, up to 32 candidates are executed, and a second adapter scores them. The score gap between result groups controls escalation to an LLM agent, optionally with candidate handoff. This is routing to another generator, not refusal of unsupported questions.

## Evaluation

BIRD standalone generation, an adapter-held-out selection split, repeated RESERVED runs, external benchmarks and 227 newly constructed questions are evaluated using reference execution agreement, latency and cost. Different experiments use Claude Code or direct API agents and different handoff designs. Main hidden-test results concern the standalone model, not the cascade.

## What the results support

Routing reduces agent calls in several settings, but its first RESERVED run fails the authors’ acceptance rule. The original candidate-handoff API cascade costs more than the API baseline on RESERVED; a later question-only variant saves cost with lower accuracy there. The fresh-set API accuracy difference is small, but this does not prove equivalent correctness.

## Limits and qualifications

Calibration, universal no-loss behavior and intrinsic answerability are not established. Development data influenced checkpoints and hard-negative design; backbone training includes BIRD train. Result equality on one database is not semantic proof. Timeout/row caps differ between systems, cost conventions vary, and public package predictions differ from scored predictions. Self-hashed registrations are not externally timestamped evidence.

## Relevance to reliable Text-to-SQL

Adjacent evidence for selective SQL generation and confidence-based escalation, with useful negative results showing why routing quality and cost need protocol-specific evaluation.
